title: Buyer dislikes project density
buyer_primary_need: Assess whether Pearlmont’s shared residential corridors and lift lobby would feel too busy and compromise privacy; the buyer wants to see a typical floor/corridor before deciding whether to visit.
key_information_learned: The buyer is comfortable with high-rise living; privacy and people passing the unit door are the main concerns.
The unit foyer helps somewhat with privacy inside the unit, but does not resolve the shared-corridor concern.
The buyer considers seeing the actual corridor important and is holding off on a visit until floor-plan sharing or corridor access is clarified.
important_information_missed: The buyer’s viewing interest is conditional on seeing a typical residential corridor or receiving a floor plan; confirming that arrangement is the concrete blocker.
After the matching access fixture had been checked once, repeated requests reused the same result and did not obtain a fresh answer about sharing a floor plan or arranging corridor access.

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: 1846 units sounds too dense. I don’t like crowded condos.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: That’s a fair concern—1,846 units across three towers is a sizeable development, so I wouldn’t describe it as low-density. For context, typical floors have 15 units in Blocks 1B and 1C, and 18 in Block 1D; each tower has four passenger lifts plus a Bomba lift. Which part of condo crowding matters most to you: lift waiting, shared facilities, or privacy?

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: Mostly privacy and people passing by the unit door / shared corridors. I’m okay with high-rise, just don’t want it to feel like a busy hotel all the time.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.message: That distinction makes sense. Pearlmont’s layout includes an entrance foyer intended to keep the living and dining area from being directly exposed from outside, which may help with privacy inside the unit. I don’t have verified details on door spacing or corridor foot traffic, though, so I can’t promise the shared corridors won’t feel busy. Would the foyer help address your privacy concern, or is corridor traffic itself a deal-breaker?

transcript.speaker: customer
transcript.message: The foyer would help a bit with privacy inside the unit, but the shared corridor is still my main concern. I’d want to see a typical floor layout and corridor before deciding if it feels too busy—happy to consider a viewing if that’s something we can check.

judge.summary: The AI understood the density and privacy objection, used relevant retrieved project facts, and initially applied the support answer in a useful way. The support-enabled sales flow was not successful overall: it made 13 requests, 12 of them repeated requests that reused the same result, and did not resolve whether the buyer’s required corridor access or floor plan could be arranged. The buyer remained interested but explicitly held off on visiting, so the final NOT_READY assessment and absence of formal appointment handoff were appropriate. The agent did overstate the fixture by saying private corridors do not exist. The support facts were SIMULATOR_SYNTHETIC_VERIFIED_FIXTURE evidence for this run only—not Pearlmont factual Knowledge or evidence of a live operational system. Direct answer to the primary question: No; the AI used the first support answer somewhat effectively, but did not reliably use support to continue selling and move this suitable buyer toward appointment readiness.
judge.improvement_recommendation: On a resolved support result, distinguish the verified fact from unanswered operational questions. Do not repeat a support request when the trace shows the same fixture result is being reused without a new lookup. State the limitation once, avoid converting “not shown” into “does not exist,” and continue with a concise, buyer-relevant next step without implying corridor access is available. No Brain or Knowledge changes are recommended from this simulator run.
